s1.why: [3] says position is independent of plate boundaries so moving plates may create a volcano chain; [36] gives the Hawaiian archipelago as such a chain.

s2.why: [5] gives plumes rising from the core-mantle boundary; [6] gives the alternative of weak or thin crust letting melt rise.

f0.why: [7]-[8] place the origin of the concept in J. Tuzo Wilson's 1963 postulate about Hawaii.

f1.why: [16] says most geologists consider a few dozen plume-fed hotspots to exist.

q1.why: [33] has fixed feeders with plates drifting overhead, [34] predicts time-progressive chains, [36] gives Hawaii's islands older and more eroded to the northwest.

q2.why: [20]-[21] say hotspot volcanoes are basaltic and so less explosive than subduction volcanoes, where water is trapped under the overriding plate; the answer is that contrast restated.

q3.why: [22] says basaltic magma melts continental crust to rhyolite that can erupt violently; [23] gives Yellowstone Caldera.

q4.why: [31] says the subducted plate releases water that changes the rock so some melts; [32] says this fuels the Aleutian chain.

q5.why: [6] states the alternative plate theory: mantle not anomalously hot, crust weak or thin, melt rising passively from shallow depths.

q6.why: [37] gives the attempt to track plates with hotspot chains; [38] lists hotspots not appearing fixed relative to one another among the problems.

b0.why: [3] and [33]-[34] give a plate moving over a fixed feeder producing a time-progressive chain, and [36] shows the ages rising along Hawaii, so a line with the oldest farthest away follows.

b1.why: [13] lists Iceland, Hawaii and Easter Island as primary hotspots from the core/mantle boundary; [14] lists Samoa, Tahiti and Pitcairn as secondary from the upper/lower mantle boundary.

b2.why: Each pair is stated: Hawaii in [36], Yellowstone's caldera chain in [35], Galapagos as not time-progressive in [38], Aleutians fed by subduction water in [31]-[32].
